name: Agent Hardening Sprint
one_liner: Fixed-fee red team of a small company's coding agents, MCP servers and CI agent jobs, then hardening through vendor-native managed settings, sandboxing and tested guardrails.

buyer.role: CTO / VP Engineering; co-signed by the SOC 2 or ISO 27001 evidence owner when a customer questionnaire or auditor has asked about AI coding tools
buyer.company_profile: B2B SaaS company with 15-150 employees whose developers use Claude Code, Cursor or Copilot with MCP servers wired to GitHub, cloud and production data, and that runs agents in CI on issue/PR events; selling to enterprises and receiving security questionnaires about AI tooling; no in-house AppSec engineer. Best fit: already on Claude Teams/Enterprise, Cursor Enterprise or an MDM, so controls can be delivered centrally.

user: Engineering leads and the platform/DevOps owner who receive the reproducible findings and apply the hardening; developers who work under the managed settings; the compliance owner who files the findings, the control description and the re-test results.

problem.summary: Small companies adopted coding agents, MCP servers and CI agent jobs faster than they set rules for them. MCP tools are auto-approved, headless runs approve everything, secrets reach tool inputs, and nobody has tested whether a poisoned issue or tool output can make their agents act. Enterprise platforms sell through large annual commits and leading MCP governance vendors offer no self-serve. These companies need their real exposure shown and the cheap native controls set up correctly.

evidence.claim: A desktop app passed blanket --allowedTools for all user-registered MCP servers, so user-added servers got tool auto-approval in headless Claude runs.
Wildcard subagents inherited all 16 MCP servers including mail-send and file-delete, and every MCP call default-allowed because the validator did not exist.
Passing secrets as raw input to an MCP tool is a security anti-pattern found in a widely used developer platform.
An MCP database server's 'read-only' mode could be bypassed (improper access control), so a configured safety mode did not hold.
Users want hooks to stop secrets leaving the machine to the LLM provider and to attackers.
A static capability audit of an MCP server found tools with no operation filtering and SQL tools accepting arbitrary DDL/DML.
Leading MCP governance vendors (Runlayer, MintMCP) publish no prices and offer no self-serve, so small teams cannot evaluate or buy.
External audit connectors and fine-grained authorization require Descope Growth at $799/mo; lower tiers keep audit for 1 week to 1 month.

why_now.summary: Coding agents now ship enforceable building blocks that small companies leave unconfigured: Claude Code server-managed settings (Teams/Enterprise) and MDM-delivered endpoint settings, native sandboxing, and blocking pre-tool hooks in Cursor, Copilot and Gemini CLI. GitHub Agentic Workflows makes read-only CI agents a documented pattern. OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications (Dec 2025) gives buyers a reference list, and compliance platforms (Vanta AI governance, Drata AI Agent Governance, Aug 2026) are teaching SOC 2 buyers to ask about agents. SOC 2 still has no AI criteria, so this is customer-questionnaire pull, not a mandate.

features.feature: Client-run inventory script that reports which agents, permission modes, hooks, MCP servers and CI agent jobs are in use, emitting only a summary (server names, permission modes, trigger types; no env values, tokens or code) that the client reviews before sharing; CI workflows also checked with zizmor
features.why: Scopes the engagement in a day without the founder ever holding client secrets; reuses a maintained scanner for workflow risks (D7).

features.feature: Prompt-injection red team run in a disposable environment: a fork of a real repo, scoped test tokens and the client's real MCP server versions or mock MCP servers, using a versioned private suite of 30+ injection cases (planted issues, poisoned files, malicious tool output, interpreter and script-file indirection). Production credentials only with written approval and least-privilege tokens
features.why: The part no platform bundles and the founder's offensive skills fit; the disposable setup keeps liability and access requests manageable while reproducing the real agent configuration.

features.feature: CI agent hardening: least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN, no secrets on untrusted triggers, read-only agent jobs with writes through a separate gated step (GitHub Agentic Workflows pattern), plus a canary secret as a tripwire only
features.why: The deterministic, low-liability fix for the main injection path; the canary is described as catching verbatim leaks only.

features.feature: Hardening through vendor-native central controls: managed settings via Claude Teams/Enterprise or MDM (allowManagedHooksOnly, managed MCP allowlist), native sandbox with network egress allowlist, and fail-closed hooks using a maintained open-source command guard where the native rules fall short; no custom policy compiler
features.why: Central, fail-closed delivery is what makes controls hold; native and maintained tools cut the upkeep a solo founder cannot carry across four agents.

features.feature: Findings report with re-test results, a stated-bypass list for every guardrail, and a control description mapped to OWASP agentic risks that the client's auditor can evaluate; agent logs shipped to the client's own central store where one exists
features.why: Gives the compliance owner an honest artefact for questionnaires without claiming a SOC 2 criterion or calling bypassable controls 'enforced'.

features.feature: Quarterly re-test: re-run the injection suite against the client's setup after agent, MCP or workflow changes, with a short delta report
features.why: Recurring revenue tied to testing, which a $15/user policy tool does not do, instead of selling policy upkeep that native settings and Kirin cover.

out_of_scope: Building a hosted SaaS platform or a cross-agent policy compiler in year one
Continuous runtime enforcement or dashboards (recommend Kirin, Vanta or the vendor's managed settings)
Holding or reviewing client logs; 24/7 monitoring or incident response
Testing third-party MCP servers or SaaS APIs the client cannot authorise
Security of the client's own AI product (LLM app pentests)
Formal SOC 2 audit, attestation or a statement that a criterion is met
Unsolicited scanning of or outreach about other companies' public repositories

competitors.name: Vanta AI governance (and the free agentic controls it publishes)
competitors.how_we_differ: Discovery, guardrails and evidence inside the SOC 2 platform the buyer already pays for; we do not compete on that. We red-team the client's real agent and CI setup and configure the native controls, and work as an implementation partner where Vanta is in place.

competitors.name: Drata AI Agent Governance
competitors.how_we_differ: Limited-availability proxy and evidence feed aimed at enterprises running Anthropic agents; no hands-on injection testing of developer toolchains or CI jobs.

competitors.name: Knostic Kirin
competitors.how_we_differ: Self-serve continuous policy and audit at $15/user/month; we recommend it for ongoing enforcement and sell what it does not do: adversarial testing, CI hardening and periodic re-tests.

competitors.name: Coding-agent security boutiques (Christian Schneider assessment, Appsecco MCP pentests)
competitors.how_we_differ: Schneider's is an interview-based assessment and roadmap; Appsecco tests MCP servers. We run hands-on injection tests against the client's own agent, MCP and CI setup and install the fixes, at a published fixed price for small companies.

competitors.name: Native managed settings plus free tools (zizmor, GitHub Agentic Workflows, open-source command guards)
competitors.how_we_differ: Free but someone has to choose, configure and test them against the client's real setup; we use them rather than replace them.

competitors.name: Pillar Security / Lasso Security
competitors.how_we_differ: Enterprise platforms bought through annual commits; we are a fixed-fee engagement priced for small companies.

competitors.name: Runlayer / MintMCP
competitors.how_we_differ: Enterprise MCP gateways with quote-only pricing; we harden the setup without adding a gateway.

differentiation: A hands-on prompt-injection red team of the client's own coding agents, MCP servers and CI jobs, followed by hardening with vendor-native central controls and re-tests, at a published fixed price. Platforms (Vanta, Drata, Kirin) discover and enforce but do not attack your setup; boutiques interview or test MCP servers in isolation. We complement the platform the buyer already has. The asset is a private, growing injection-test suite and public research, not a policy kit.

build.team: 1 technical founder (solo, bootstrapped); white-label partners do their own selling; subcontract a tester only above 2 sprints per month
hardest_parts: Building credibility first: 2-3 public reproducible write-ups on coding-agent or CI-agent injection (ideally vendor-acknowledged findings) before selling, since the founder's track record is Windows detection and CTFs
Building the disposable test environment and the versioned injection suite (including interpreter and script-file indirection) so red teams are reproducible and safe in a 2-week sprint
Keeping hardening guidance and the test suite current as four agents change managed-settings, sandbox and hook semantics, including cloud and CI agent limitations
Engagement paperwork and cover: rules of engagement, authorisation letter, liability cap, DPA, and E&O/cyber insurance before the first sprint
Finding buyers without paid ads or an existing client base

pricing.model: Fixed-fee red team and hardening sprint, then optional quarterly re-test; wholesale price for partner firms that resell it
pricing.entry_price: $6,500 fixed fee for up to 25 developers and 3 CI repositories (2-week sprint: inventory, red team, CI hardening, native-control setup, re-test); quarterly re-test $1,800; partners buy at $5,000
pricing.rationale: Priced as a scoped assessment rather than a tool: well under enterprise annual commits (Lasso $20k+), about a year of Descope Growth, and in a different category from $15-25/user tools, which the concept recommends rather than undercuts. At about 2 sprints a month (realistic solo capacity) this grosses about $13k/month and covers insurance and a partner margin. Re-tests are priced on testing, not policy upkeep, so they do not compete with Kirin.

comparables.price: AWS Marketplace annual commit $20,000 (GenAI Chatbots), $50,000 (LLM gateway)

go_to_market.first_customers: Ten 15-150 person B2B SaaS companies using coding agents with MCP servers and CI agent jobs that have a concrete trigger: an enterprise customer questionnaire item on AI coding tools, an auditor question, or an internal near-miss. Reached through the founder's contacts, readers of the public research, and two or three SOC 2 readiness, vCISO or small pentest firms that add the sprint as their 'AI coding tools' line item.
go_to_market.channel: Research-led and partner-led: public write-ups, a self-scan-only release of the inventory tool and BSides/meetup talks build credibility; small pentest, SOC 2 readiness and vCISO firms resell the sprint at the wholesale price (their margin about $1.5k); listing in compliance-platform partner directories where available. Vulnerabilities found in public projects during research go through a published, no-pitch private disclosure policy, never into sales.
go_to_market.wedge: A free, client-run self-scan plus a 30-minute walkthrough of its summary, ending with a fixed quote; or a one-repository CI-agent injection test as the first paid step for buyers unsure about granting red-team access.

risks: Demand: SOC 2 has no AI criteria, so purchases depend on customer questionnaires, auditor questions or incidents; without them, small CTOs defer and deal flow is uneven.

Bundling: Vanta, Drata and Kirin bundle discovery, guardrails and evidence, and agent vendors expand managed settings; the configuration part shrinks, leaving the red team and re-tests as the defensible core. No technical moat; reputation and the private test suite are the only assets.
Credibility and capacity: an unknown solo founder competes with boutiques that already publish research; about 2 sprints a month caps revenue until partners or a second tester are added.

Liability and data: injection tests can cause damage if production credentials are used; needs written authorisation, third-party exclusions, a liability cap, insurance, and testing in disposable environments by default. The founder must stay out of client logs, and command logging is employee monitoring that needs notice.

Misrepresentation: guardrails are client-side and partly fail-open; they must be described with stated bypasses, never as 'enforced' or as meeting a SOC 2 criterion, or a client incident becomes a claim against the founder.

Technical: hooks and command parsing do not stop interpreter or script indirection; real containment depends on sandboxing, egress limits and least-privilege tokens, which some clients will not adopt.

riskiest_assumption.assumption: Enough 15-150 person SaaS companies have a concrete trigger (a customer questionnaire item, auditor question or near-miss about coding agents) to pay about $6,500 for a red team and hardening now, directly or through a partner firm.
riskiest_assumption.test: In two weeks: interview 10 SOC 2 readiness, vCISO or small pentest firms about how often clients get coding-agent or MCP questions and offer them the wholesale sprint; contact 20 CTOs from the founder's network and research readers, ask whether they have such a request in writing, and offer a pre-sold sprint with a $1,000 deposit.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: At least 3 of 10 partner firms report clients with written coding-agent questions and 2 agree in writing to refer or resell, and at least 1 CTO pays a deposit at $6,500 (or 2 at the one-repository CI test).

open_questions: How fast will questionnaire and auditor questions about coding agents become routine, and in which customer segments first?
Will Vanta or Drata partner programmes accept a solo implementation partner, or build their own red-team service?
What share of target companies already have Claude Teams/Enterprise, Cursor Enterprise or MDM, so controls can be delivered centrally?
Can E&O and cyber cover be bought at a cost the sprint price absorbs for a new solo firm?
Can a later detection add-on (alerts on agent-spawned shells and MCP processes) use the founder's detection-engineering strength on mostly macOS/Linux fleets?
Which repeated work, such as the injection suite, could become a self-serve product?
revision_log: [variant v2] Headless/CI coverage in the policy pack: read-only default for CI agent runs, automatic downgrade when the job input is untrusted issue/PR text, and a planted canary secret that fails the run if it appears in tool input or output

[variant v2] Agent-workflow scanner: reads .github/workflows and flags agent steps triggered by untrusted events with write permissions or secrets; used in the inventory and, on public repos, as an outbound lead source

[variant v1] Hook scripts evaluate commands by parsing them (shell AST) instead of string patterns, and the kit keeps one YAML policy compiled into each agent's native hook/policy format as the path to a later product
[judge] Dropped the Pillar $175,000 comparable and its mention in the rationale: the fact-checker flagged it as a whole-platform price, not a coding-agent product price

[competitor-analyst] Vanta (acquiring Pillar) and Drata bundle agent discovery, guardrails and evidence → repositioned as a red-team and hardening service that complements these platforms and acts as their implementation partner; both added to competitors and why_now; continuous enforcement moved out of scope

[competitor-analyst] Knostic Kirin at ~$375/month matches the $400 retainer → policy-upkeep retainer dropped; replaced by a quarterly re-test ($1,800) that Kirin does not offer; Kirin recommended for ongoing enforcement

[competitor-analyst] Boutiques (Christian Schneider, Appsecco) already sell coding-agent/MCP assessments → added to competitors; differentiation narrowed to hands-on injection testing of the client's own agent, MCP and CI setup plus installed fixes at a published small-company price

[competitor-analyst] zizmor and GitHub Agentic Workflows cover CI scanning and read-only agent jobs → custom workflow scanner replaced by zizmor and the gh-aw pattern; CI value now in configuring and testing them

[defensibility] Fatal: platform owners keep bundling the configuration work → partly accepted: configuration is no longer the core; the red team and re-tests are. Not changed on 'no-go': a solo services business needs paying clients, not a technical moat, and bundled controls still need someone to attack and verify them; risk stated plainly
[defensibility] Shell-AST hook scripts already exist free (open-source command guards) → custom parser and policy compiler dropped; maintained OSS guards and native controls used instead (D7)
[defensibility] Open-source kit gives away the only asset → injection test suite kept private and versioned; only the self-scan inventory tool is released
[defensibility] Channel partners are likeliest copiers → partners now resell at a wholesale price ($5,000) so the sprint is their line item rather than a competitor's

[economic-buyer] No must-have trigger; SOC 2 has no AI criteria → buyer narrowed to companies with a written questionnaire item, auditor question or near-miss; riskiest assumption and test now target the trigger; CSA source added to why_now
[economic-buyer] No budget line; buyers prefer existing pentest or compliance vendors → channel shifted to those vendors as resellers

[economic-buyer] Red-team approval friction exceeds price → disposable-environment testing by default, a one-repository CI test as a lower-friction first step, and engagement paperwork plus insurance listed as pre-launch work
[founder-fit] Credibility gap and three new domains; 1-month MVP unrealistic → months_to_mvp raised to 3 with 2-3 public write-ups before selling
[founder-fit] First-customer plan exceeds solo reach → success signal reset to partner commitments and one deposit; first revenue expected around month 3-5
[founder-fit] Capacity is ~2 sprints a month, not 3-4 → pricing rationale now assumes 2 per month
[founder-fit] Windows detection strengths unused → not changed in v1 (target fleets are mostly macOS/Linux); a detection add-on kept as an open question
[gtm-pricing] $3,500 below pentest floor and unit economics don't close → entry price raised to $6,500 for a defined scope; partners at $5,000
[gtm-pricing] Retainer will churn against Kirin and free managed settings → retainer replaced by quarterly re-test
[gtm-pricing] Cold exposure notes convert poorly and a stranger's inventory script is a trust ask → exposure notes removed; inventory runs client-side and emits a reviewed summary only
[gtm-pricing] Little room to expand → not changed beyond re-tests and partner volume; expansion via a later product left as an open question
[legal-ethics] Outbound exposure notes look like vulnerability-for-sale → channel dropped; replaced by a published no-pitch disclosure policy; unsolicited scanning listed out of scope

[legal-ethics] Injection testing against production-credentialed agents → disposable fork, scoped test tokens and mock MCP servers by default; production only with written approval; authorisation letter, third-party exclusion, liability cap and insurance in hardest_parts and risks; third-party MCP/SaaS testing out of scope

[legal-ethics] Data custody and employee monitoring → founder never holds client logs (out of scope); inventory emits a summary without env values; logs stay in the client's store; DPA and employee notice in risks

[legal-ethics] 'Enforced' and SOC 2 wording is misrepresentation → one-liner and features now say guardrails with a stated-bypass list and a control description the auditor evaluates; formal attestation and criterion claims out of scope
[legal-ethics] Dual-use workflow scanner → only a self-scan mode is released; CI scanning uses zizmor

[market-skeptic] Evidence from the wrong people; #60246 filed by an MCP-governance vendor → removed #60246 from problem.evidence and added two incident-style issues (headless MCP auto-approval, MCP read-only bypass); buyer-side demand still unproven and tested by the riskiest assumption

[market-skeptic] Buyers' budgeted pain is insecure generated code → not changed: that budget belongs to SAST/SCA incumbents; this concept targets the narrower questionnaire-triggered segment and says demand is secondary in risks
[market-skeptic] Reachable slice is narrow → not changed: low thousands of companies is enough for a solo services firm doing ~24 sprints a year

[security-practitioner] Per-laptop hooks are client-side and bypassable → controls delivered through server-managed settings (Teams/Enterprise) or MDM endpoint settings; best-fit buyers are those with central delivery; others told their guardrails are advisory

[security-practitioner] Hooks fail open and miss script/interpreter indirection → fail-closed hooks only where needed, native sandbox with egress allowlist added, indirection cases added to the injection suite and re-test
[security-practitioner] Access request hard to grant → disposable environment by default and client-run inventory without secrets
[security-practitioner] Canary catches only verbatim leaks → canary demoted to a tripwire; least-privilege tokens and no secrets on untrusted triggers are the primary CI fix
[security-practitioner] Local logs are tamper-prone → logs shipped to the client's central store where one exists; no claim of tamper-resistant evidence otherwise

[technical-feasibility] Policy compiler across four agents is a maintenance burden with silent holes → compiler dropped; per-agent native controls documented with a coverage matrix and stated gaps (cloud/CI agent limitations)
[technical-feasibility] Disposable test environment not budgeted → added as an MVP feature and a hardest part; months_to_mvp raised to 3
